title: Eighteen Months in Corinth
sum: Paul arrives in Corinth alone, finds work and lodging with Aquila and Priscilla, Jewish believers expelled from Rome by Claudius, and argues in the synagogue every Sabbath. When Silas and Timothy come, he gives himself wholly to preaching. Opposition drives him next door, to the house of a God-fearer, but the synagogue's leader Crispus believes with his household. In a night vision the Lord tells Paul not to be afraid, for he has "a large people" in the city. Paul stays a year and a half.

The Jewish community brings Paul before the new proconsul, Gallio, who refuses to judge what he sees as a dispute about Jewish law. Paul then sails for Syria with Priscilla and Aquila, cuts his hair because of a vow, leaves the couple at Ephesus, visits Jerusalem and Antioch, and sets out again through Galatia and Phrygia. Meanwhile Apollos, a learned Jew from Alexandria, teaches about Jesus at Ephesus knowing only John's baptism. Priscilla and Aquila take him aside and teach him more accurately, and he goes on to Corinth with the church's letter of welcome.
readings: Corinth is where Acts can best be checked against outside evidence: Claudius' expulsion of the Jews (Suetonius), Gallio's year as proconsul (the Delphi inscription), the bēma in the forum, and the names Crispus, Sosthenes, Gaius and Erastus in Paul's own letters. Most historians, including many who doubt other parts of Acts, accept the outline of this chapter and use it to date Paul's career.

Luke builds the chapter on two promises and their fulfillment: the Lord's "no one will lay a hand on you to do you harm" (18:10) is kept when a Roman governor throws out the case against Paul (18:14–16), and the turn "to the Gentiles" (18:6) is balanced by a synagogue leader's faith (18:8). The chapter also passes the baton: Paul leaves, and others (Priscilla, Aquila, Apollos) carry the work on.

views.H: The chapter is one of the best anchored in Acts. Claudius' edict (AD 49 by Orosius' date) explains why a Jewish couple from Rome was in Corinth; Gallio's proconsulship (about 51–52) fixes the end of Paul's stay. Tentmaking, the synagogue next door, the bēma, the port of Cenchreae and the sea route to Ephesus all fit the city as archaeology shows it.
views.C: Critical scholars note how neatly the Gallio scene serves Luke's purpose: a Roman official declares the faith an internal Jewish matter, not a crime. Some think Luke compressed two visits to Corinth or two hearings into one story. Paul's letters confirm many details (Crispus, Sosthenes, Paul working with his hands, money from Macedonia) but never mention Gallio, Aquila's expulsion or Paul's vow. The quick trip in 18:22 is hard to match with Galatians, and its purpose is debated.
views.L: Corinth repeats the pattern of Acts 13–17: synagogue first, opposition, a turn to the Gentiles, and protection by Roman officials. But the Lord's vision (18:9–10) slows the pace, and Paul stays. The second half is a hinge: Paul's travel summary (18:18–23) closes his work in the Aegean and opens the long Ephesian chapter, while Apollos' story prepares for the disciples of John in 19:1–7.
views.J: The chapter is full of Jews: Aquila and Priscilla, expelled with the rest of Rome's Jews; Crispus and Sosthenes, synagogue leaders; Apollos of Alexandria, mighty in the Scriptures; and Paul himself, who cuts his hair under a vow. The dispute before Gallio is an argument among Jews about their own Scriptures and their Messiah. Jewish scholars such as Paula Fredriksen and Mark Nanos read Paul as a Jew who kept his ancestral practices among Jews, a picture this chapter supports.
views.T: Preachers have used the vision (18:9–10) to encourage pastors in hard places, and Gallio's indifference (18:17) as a warning against careless faith, though Luke's point was different. Priscilla's teaching of Apollos (18:26) was praised by John Chrysostom and is central to modern debates over women teaching. Preachers from Chrysostom on have held up Paul the tentmaker as a model of humble, self-supporting ministry.

deep.h: Acts and Paul's letters at Corinth
deep.b:
Corinth is the place where Acts and Paul's letters overlap most, and they agree on a surprising number of small things, without either copying the other:

  • Crispus, synagogue leader in Acts 18:8, is one of only two Corinthians Paul baptized himself (1 Corinthians 1:14).
  • Sosthenes, beaten before Gallio (18:17), is named with Paul at the start of 1 Corinthians (1 Corinthians 1:1), perhaps the same man.
  • Silas and Timothy arrive from Macedonia (18:5); 1 Thessalonians, written from Corinth, names both (1 Thessalonians 1:1; 3:6), and Paul says believers from Macedonia supplied his needs there (2 Corinthians 11:9).
  • Paul's trade (18:3) matches his repeated statements that he worked with his own hands (1 Corinthians 4:12; 9:6–18).
  • Apollos (18:24–28) appears in 1 Corinthians 1–4 as a much-admired teacher who followed Paul.
  • Priscilla and Aquila appear in Ephesus with a church in their house (1 Corinthians 16:19) and later in Rome (Romans 16:3–5).

There are also gaps: Paul's letters never mention Gallio or the vow, and Acts never mentions the letters. Scholars who trust Acts take the agreements as signs of good sources; skeptics answer that Luke may have known some of Paul's letters. Most think the agreements are too incidental for that.

Paul's letters give almost no dates, so Gallio's year in Achaia (see the note on 18:12) is the anchor for the whole chronology of his life. If Gallio governed from mid-51 to mid-52, and Paul had been in Corinth some months when he was brought before him, then Paul arrived about early 50 and left in 51 or 52. That fits Orosius' date of AD 49 for Claudius' edict, which brought Aquila and Priscilla to Corinth "just" before Paul (18:2). Counting back with Galatians 1:18 and 2:1 ("after three years," "after fourteen years") places Paul's call in the early to mid-30s; counting forward with Acts 19–24 places his arrest in Jerusalem about 57. Scholars differ by a year or two at almost every step, and some reject Orosius' date (he names Josephus as his source, but no such passage is in Josephus' surviving works), but nearly all chronologies of Paul start here.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the haircut and the promise
deep.b: Luke gives no reason for Paul's vow (18:18), and he places it right after the one stretch in Acts where a promise of God is fulfilled point by point: "Have no fear... no one will lay a hand on you to do you harm" (18:9–10), followed by a hearing in which the case collapses and someone else is beaten instead (18:12–17). My suggestion is that the vow was a vow of thanks for that protection, made in fear when the vision came and completed when Paul left the city safely. Jews made vows in danger and fulfilled them when delivered (Psalm 66:13–14; Jonah 2:9; compare the vow of Jacob, Genesis 28:20–22). The cut hair at Cenchreae would mark the end of the vow's period, with the offering to follow in Jerusalem (18:22). Commentators have suggested a vow of thanks for safety before; tying it to the specific promise of 18:10 is my own reading. Luke does not say it.

echoes: Isaiah 41:10; Isaiah 43:5; Jeremiah 1:8; Joshua 1:9; Ezekiel 33:1–9; Numbers 6:1–21; 2 Samuel 1:16; Acts 13:46; Acts 28:28; 1 Corinthians 1:1; 1 Corinthians 1:12–17; 1 Corinthians 2:1–5; 1 Corinthians 3:4–6; 1 Thessalonians 3:6; Romans 16:3–5; Romans 16:23

settings.what: Paul's teaching in the synagogue at Corinth
settings.to: the Jews and God-fearing Greeks of Corinth's synagogue, Sabbath after Sabbath
settings.when: on his arrival in Corinth, about AD 50, while he worked at his trade during the week
settings.why: to persuade fellow Jews and the Gentiles who worshiped with them that the Messiah Israel awaited is Jesus, arguing from the Scriptures they shared
settings.readers: Luke's readers (Theophilus and the churches he wrote for) saw the pattern of Acts at work: the good news goes to the synagogue first, as Jesus' did, because it is Israel's own hope.

settings.to: the Jews of the Corinthian synagogue who opposed and insulted him
settings.when: after Silas and Timothy arrived and Paul began preaching full time
settings.why: to declare, with a gesture and words from the prophets, that he had done his duty as a watchman and was now free to preach to Gentiles in the city; not a curse, and not the end of his work with Jews (he moves next door, and the synagogue leader believes)
settings.readers: For Luke's readers, many of them Gentiles, the scene explained how churches like theirs came to meet in houses next to synagogues rather than in them.
views: Paul leaves this synagogue only; he keeps going to Jews first elsewhere (18:19; 19:8). Jervell and many others.
Each turn (13:46; 18:6; 28:28) marks a growing break between the church and the Jewish people. Jack Sanders and others.

settings.by: the Lord (most likely the risen Jesus, as in 9:10–17 and 23:11)
settings.to: Paul, alone, by night in Corinth
settings.when: after the break with the synagogue, as opposition grew
settings.why: to end Paul's fear and keep him in the city: the Lord promises his presence, protection, and a large "people" still to be gathered there
settings.readers: Luke's readers (Theophilus and the churches he wrote for) learned that the spread of the church was the Lord's own work, and heard the same "Have no fear; I am with you" that the prophets had heard.

settings.by: the Jews of Corinth, acting together
settings.to: Gallio, proconsul of Achaia, at the bēma in the forum
settings.when: about AD 51–52, perhaps early in Gallio's term (accusers often tested a new governor), though Luke does not say
settings.why: to get a Roman ruling against Paul by presenting his teaching as an illegal way of worshiping God, and so to stop his work in the city
settings.readers: For Luke's readers the charge was a test case: what would Rome say about the new movement?
views: The complaint was that Paul broke the law of Moses, and they wanted Rome to back the synagogue's authority.
The complaint was that Paul promoted an unlawful religion, a matter for the governor.

settings.to: the Jewish accusers, before Paul could speak
settings.when: at the same hearing
settings.why: to refuse the case: a Roman governor would judge crimes, not quarrels about "a word and names" and someone else's law
settings.readers: The ruling was precious to Luke's readers. A brother of Seneca, a senior official of Rome, had treated Christian preaching as a matter for Jews to settle, not a crime; Luke may hope that later officials would follow the precedent.

settings.to: the Jews of the Ephesian synagogue who asked him to stay
settings.when: on his first, brief stop in Ephesus, on the way to Syria
settings.why: to decline their invitation for now while promising, God willing, to return
settings.readers: Luke's readers knew how the promise was kept: chapter 19 tells of Paul's longest stay anywhere.

settings.what: Apollos' teaching, and Priscilla and Aquila's instruction
settings.to: the synagogue at Ephesus; then Apollos himself, privately
settings.when: while Paul was away in Syria and Galatia, about AD 52
settings.why: Apollos meant to show from the Scriptures that the Messiah is Jesus; Priscilla and Aquila meant to complete what he knew, especially about baptism, without shaming him in public
settings.readers: Luke's readers (Theophilus and the churches he wrote for) saw the church's teaching passed on by lay believers, a woman among them, and a gifted newcomer welcomed and corrected rather than rejected.
views: The couple taught him at home; the scene sets no pattern for public teaching. Complementarian readers.
Priscilla, named first, taught a learned man the faith; the scene supports women's teaching. Egalitarian readers.

settings.what: The Ephesian believers' letter of recommendation
settings.to: the disciples in Achaia, chiefly Corinth
settings.when: when Apollos decided to cross to Achaia
settings.why: to vouch for Apollos so that the Corinthian church would receive him as a trusted teacher
settings.readers: Luke's readers knew such letters well: churches in different cities trusted each other through them (2 Corinthians 3:1; Romans 16:1–2).

settings.to: the Jews of Achaia, chiefly at Corinth, out in public
settings.when: after he crossed from Ephesus with the believers' letter, about AD 52
settings.why: to prove from the Scriptures, before anyone who would listen, that the Messiah is Jesus, and so to strengthen the young church Paul had left behind
settings.readers: Luke's readers saw Paul's work carried on by another gifted teacher. Paul's own letter says the same in a picture: he planted and Apollos watered (1 Corinthians 3:6).

title: The Word Grows Strong in Ephesus
sum: Paul returns to Ephesus, as he promised, and meets about twelve disciples who know only John's baptism and have never heard that the Holy Spirit has come. He teaches them about Jesus; they are baptized into his name, and when Paul lays hands on them the Spirit comes, and they speak in tongues and prophesy. Paul teaches in the synagogue for three months and then, for two years, daily in the school of Tyrannus, until the word has spread across the province of Asia.

God does unusual miracles through Paul, even through his work clothes. Seven sons of a Jewish high priest try to use Jesus' name as a spell and are beaten by the man they meant to free. Fear falls on the city; believers confess their magical practices and burn their books, worth fifty thousand silver coins. Paul plans his journey to Jerusalem and then Rome. Then the silversmith Demetrius rouses the craftsmen who make shrines of Artemis, and the city pours into the theater chanting "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!" for two hours, until the city's chief clerk calms the crowd and sends the assembly home.
readings: Ephesus as Luke describes it matches what inscriptions and ruins show: the theater, the Asiarchs, the chief clerk, the title "temple warden," the silver images of Artemis, the city's fame for magic, and Rome's fear of riots. Paul's letters confirm a long, hard stay here (1 Corinthians 16:8–9; 15:32; 2 Corinthians 1:8–10). Historians debate the miracle stories and the role of the Jewish exorcists, and they note that Paul was probably in more danger at Ephesus than Luke tells.

The chapter is a contest of powers. The Holy Spirit comes with visible signs; the name of Jesus heals in God's hands but backfires when used as magic; books of spells go up in flames; and the great goddess of the city is defended only by a mob and a clerk's speech. Luke closes the section with a summary (19:20) and turns the whole book toward Jerusalem and Rome (19:21).

Churches have drawn on this chapter for teaching on the Holy Spirit and baptism (19:1–7), for practices of healing and prayer cloths (19:11–12), for warnings against the occult (19:13–19), and for the courage of believers facing a hostile culture (19:23–41). The cards below show where the churches disagree.

views.H: Ephesus was the capital of Asia and the home of one of the seven wonders. The details of the riot (the theater, the Asiarchs, the clerk of the people, the lawful assembly, the proconsuls and court days) fit first-century Ephesus closely; Sherwin-White judged them accurate. The Salutaris inscription (AD 104) shows silver images of Artemis carried into the theater at assemblies.
views.C: Critical scholars ask whether 19:1–7 reflects a real rival movement around John the Baptist that Luke folds into the church (Käsemann). Ernst Haenchen and Richard Pervo saw the riot as a skillfully told scene with little history behind it; Colin Hemer and others answered that its local color is too exact to be invented. Paul's letters speak of deadly danger in Asia (2 Corinthians 1:8–10), which Luke does not narrate; some think Paul was imprisoned in Ephesus.
views.L: Luke shapes the chapter in panels: Spirit (19:1–7), word (19:8–10), power and its counterfeit (19:11–20), plan (19:21–22), and riot (19:23–41). The summary of 19:20 closes the Aegean mission, and 19:21, with its divine "must," opens the final third of the book, as Luke 9:51 opens Jesus' journey to Jerusalem. The word ekklēsia, "assembly," is used three times for the city's meeting, just before Paul speaks to the elders of "the church of God" (20:28).
views.J: The chapter shows Jews on several sides: Paul arguing in the synagogue, Jewish exorcists using Jesus' name, a Jewish community trying to separate itself from Paul during the riot, and Jews and Greeks together hearing the word (19:10, 17). Diaspora Jews in Ephesus had rights guaranteed by Roman decrees, and their rejection of idols put them at risk whenever the city's goddess seemed threatened. Luke's "Jewish exorcists" reflect a real ancient reputation (Josephus tells of one, Eleazar), not a picture of Judaism as such.
views.T: Catholic and Orthodox teaching sees 19:5–6 (with 8:14–17) as the root of confirmation or chrismation, and 19:11–12 as support for honoring relics. Pentecostal churches read 19:1–7 as a model of Spirit baptism after conversion, shown by tongues. Reformation churches read 19:19 as a model of repentance and used it against occult practices.

deep.h: The Spirit and baptism in Acts: no single order
deep.b:
Readers who look for one pattern of conversion in Acts find several:

  • Pentecost (2:38): repent, be baptized into the name of Jesus Christ, receive the gift of the Spirit.
  • Samaria (8:12–17): belief and baptism first; the Spirit comes later, when Peter and John lay on hands.
  • Saul (9:17–18): Ananias lays on hands that Saul may see and be filled with the Spirit; then he is baptized.
  • Cornelius (10:44–48): the Spirit falls during Peter's sermon, before baptism.
  • Ephesus (19:1–7): John's baptism, then teaching, baptism into Jesus' name, laying on of hands, and the Spirit with tongues and prophecy.

Pentecostal readers take the cases where the Spirit comes after faith (Samaria, Ephesus) as a lasting pattern. Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican readers see in the laying on of hands the beginning of confirmation. Many Protestant scholars, including James Dunn, argue that Luke tells unusual cases at turning points of the mission, and that the norm is 2:38: faith, baptism and the Spirit together. Luke himself never states a rule; he shows God giving the Spirit to every new group the gospel reaches, sometimes surprising the apostles. How the churches answer the question of a second experience of the Spirit is set out on the card at Acts 2:4.

deep.h: Magic, the name of Jesus, and the burned books
deep.b: Ephesus was known across the ancient world for magic. "Ephesian letters" were famous charms, and handbooks of spells like those burned in 19:19 survive on papyrus from Egypt: recipes for love, healing, revenge and protection, packed with the names of gods, angels and Jewish figures such as Solomon. Magic worked, people believed, by naming the right power in the right words. Luke's story draws the line between the gospel and magic carefully. God works miracles through Paul (19:11), but the name of Jesus is not a formula that anyone can borrow (19:13–16). The result is that believers give up their own magic, revealing their secret spells and burning their books (19:18–19). Simon of Samaria (8:9–24) and Bar-Jesus on Cyprus (13:6–12) are earlier scenes on the same theme.

Two views have long stood side by side. Skeptical: Ernst Haenchen and Richard Pervo saw the riot as a dramatic set piece. Paul never appears in it; it ends with a pagan official declaring the Christians innocent, which suits Luke's purpose; and it allows Paul to leave Ephesus on his own terms, though his letters suggest he faced something worse there. Historical: William Ramsay, A. N. Sherwin-White and Colin Hemer pointed to the exact local details: the Asiarchs, the clerk of the people, the title neōkoros, the use of the theater for assemblies, the "lawful assembly" held on fixed days, and the Roman threat behind the clerk's words. They argued that a writer far from Ephesus could hardly have known all this. Many scholars take a middle position: Luke had good information about a real disturbance and told it with skill to make his points about Rome and the church.

deep.title: Claude's theory: two assemblies in one city
deep.b: Luke calls the crowd in the theater an ekklēsia three times (19:32, 39, 41), the only place in Acts where the word is used of a pagan gathering, and in the very next scene Paul addresses the elders of "the church (ekklēsia) of God" (20:17, 28). I suggest that Luke places the two assemblies side by side on purpose. The city's assembly is confused, most do not know why they have met, it shouts one slogan for two hours, it is called together by a man defending his income, and it fears punishment from Rome. The church's leaders are called by the Spirit, warned with tears, bought with blood, and sent away in prayer. Several commentators have noticed the wordplay; the full contrast, point by point, is my own reading.

echoes: Isaiah 40:3; Deuteronomy 4:28; Psalm 115:4; Isaiah 44:9–20; Numbers 11:25; Matthew 3:11; Luke 3:16; Acts 2:1–4; Acts 2:38; Acts 8:9–24; Acts 8:14–17; Acts 10:44–48; Acts 13:6–12; Acts 16:16–24; 1 Corinthians 15:32; 1 Corinthians 16:8–9; 2 Corinthians 1:8–10; Ephesians 1:1; Revelation 2:1–7

settings.what: Paul questions the disciples who knew only John's baptism
settings.to: about twelve men in Ephesus who called themselves disciples
settings.when: on Paul's return to Ephesus, about AD 52
settings.why: to find out what they lacked and to show them that John's baptism had pointed to Jesus, the one coming after him, so that they might believe in him and receive the Spirit
settings.readers: Luke's readers (Theophilus and the churches he wrote for) may have known groups who honored John the Baptist; the scene showed that John's followers belonged with the church, under Jesus.
views: They believed in Jesus but had incomplete teaching, like Apollos.
They were John the Baptist's disciples, not yet Christians (Käsemann; Dunn in a different way).

settings.what: Paul's teaching in the synagogue and the school of Tyrannus
settings.to: first the synagogue of Ephesus for three months; then the disciples and any who came, daily, in a rented lecture hall
settings.when: about AD 52–55
settings.why: to persuade the Jews about the kingdom of God, and, when some hardened, to keep teaching believers and inquirers in a neutral place, so that the word could spread through the province
settings.readers: Luke's readers saw the church gaining a public, almost philosophical, face in the great city, and the word reaching Jews and Greeks alike.

settings.by: itinerant Jewish exorcists, the seven sons of Sceva
settings.to: evil spirits in people they tried to free
settings.when: while Paul's miracles were becoming known
settings.why: to borrow the power of a name that seemed to work for Paul, as exorcists borrowed many names
settings.readers: Luke's readers (Theophilus and the churches he wrote for) learned that Jesus' name is not a magic word; it belongs to those who belong to him.

settings.by: the evil spirit, speaking through the man
settings.to: the sons of Sceva
settings.when: during their attempted exorcism
settings.why: in the story, to expose the exorcists as outsiders to the power they claimed: the spirit knows Jesus and knows of Paul, but not them
settings.readers: The scene is told with humor for readers who lived among magicians and charms.

settings.to: his companions (Luke reports it as his resolve)
settings.when: after two years and more in Ephesus, about AD 55
settings.why: to set the course of the rest of his work: through Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem with the collection, and then to Rome, under God's "must"
settings.readers: For Luke's readers this sentence outlines the rest of Acts. They knew Paul reached Rome, but as a prisoner.

settings.to: the craftsmen of Ephesus who made shrines of Artemis, and workers in related trades
settings.when: near the end of Paul's stay, probably about AD 55
settings.why: to stir his fellow tradesmen to act against Paul by joining their lost income to the honor of the city's temple and its goddess
settings.readers: Luke's readers (Theophilus and the churches he wrote for) recognized a familiar mix of religion, money and civic pride, and an honest witness from a pagan that Paul's preaching against idols was changing whole cities.

settings.what: The chant: "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!"
settings.by: the craftsmen, then the crowd in the theater
settings.to: one another, the city, and the goddess
settings.when: during the riot, for about two hours
settings.why: to declare loyalty to the city's goddess and to drown out anyone who seemed to oppose her, including the Jew Alexander
settings.readers: Luke's readers would hear the chant as the opposite of true worship: loud, unanimous and empty.

settings.by: the city's chief clerk (grammateus tou dēmou)
settings.to: the crowd gathered in the theater as an unofficial assembly
settings.when: after two hours of chanting
settings.why: to calm the crowd and avoid Roman punishment: the goddess's glory is beyond doubt, the accused have committed no crime, and complaints belong in the courts or the lawful assembly
settings.readers: For Luke's readers (Theophilus and the churches he wrote for), a city's own official declared Paul's companions innocent of robbery and blasphemy, part of Luke's case that the faith was no danger to public order.

traditions.q: The disciples at Ephesus had received John's baptism, and Paul had them baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus (19:3–5). When, if ever, should a person be baptized again?
views: Never, if the first baptism was valid: baptism marks the soul with an indelible seal and cannot be repeated (Catechism 1272). John's baptism was not Christian baptism (Council of Trent, Session 7, Canons on Baptism, canon 1), so the Ephesians were baptized for the first time. Baptism given by other Christians with water and the threefold name is recognized.

Baptism is "one baptism for the forgiveness of sins" (Nicene Creed) and is not repeated. Practice in receiving converts varies: many are received by chrismation, but some Orthodox churches baptize converts whose earlier baptism they do not judge to be a true Orthodox baptism.

A baptism with water and God's word is valid even if given to an infant or without the recipient's faith at the time, and must not be repeated. Luther wrote against rebaptism (Concerning Rebaptism, 1528), and the Augsburg Confession (article 9) rejects the Anabaptists' practice.

Baptism is given once and is never repeated (Westminster Confession 28.7). Calvin held that John's baptism was the same baptism as the one the apostles gave (Institutes 4.15.7–8), so he denied that 19:5 describes a second water baptism: he took "baptized" there to mean the gift of the Spirit through the laying on of hands (4.15.18). Other Protestant interpreters read 19:5 as the end of Paul's sentence, describing John's hearers, so that no rebaptism is narrated. Baptisms given in the threefold name by other churches, infants included, are recognized.

Baptism is for those who have repented and believe (Schleitheim Confession, article 1). Infant baptism is not true baptism, so baptizing a believer who was sprinkled as a baby is not "rebaptism"; Acts 19 shows that a baptism given without faith in Christ is to be replaced.

Only the immersion of a professing believer is baptism (Second London Confession, chapter 29). Baptist churches baptize people who were baptized as infants, holding that their first baptism was not Christian baptism, much as Paul treated John's baptism here.

Baptism must be "in the name of Jesus Christ" (2:38; 19:5). People baptized with the words "Father, Son and Holy Spirit" are baptized again in Jesus' name, following the example of the Ephesian disciples.

title: Farewell at Miletus
sum: After the riot Paul leaves Ephesus, encourages the churches of Macedonia, and spends three months in Greece. A plot against him changes his route, and he returns through Macedonia with a group of delegates from his churches. The narrator's "we" returns at Philippi. At Troas, on the first day of the week, the believers gather to break bread; Paul talks until midnight, a young man named Eutychus falls asleep and drops from a third-story window, and Paul embraces him and gives him back alive. The talk and the meal go on until dawn.

Hurrying to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost, Paul sails past Ephesus and calls the church's elders to meet him at Miletus. There he gives his only speech in Acts to Christian leaders: a farewell that looks back on his three years with them, looks ahead to chains in Jerusalem, and charges them to shepherd the church of God, bought with blood, against wolves from outside and within. He reminds them that he worked with his own hands and quotes a saying of Jesus found nowhere in the Gospels: "Giving is more blessed than receiving." They kneel, pray, weep, and walk him to the ship.
readings: The travel log of 20:5–16 has the feel of a diary: day counts, islands, a walk overland, and the dates of Passover and Pentecost. Paul's letters confirm the journey's purpose (the collection) and many of the companions named in 20:4. Historians debate whether Eutychus died, and how much of the Miletus speech gives Paul's words rather than Luke's summary.

The Miletus speech is Paul's farewell, like those of Jacob, Moses, Samuel and Jesus. It defends his conduct, foresees his suffering, hands responsibility to the next leaders, and warns of false teachers. For Luke's readers, living after Paul's death, it was the apostle's last will for the churches.

The chapter gives the earliest clear picture of Christians meeting on the first day of the week to break bread, a key text for Sunday worship and for the frequency of the Lord's Supper. The charge to elders (20:28) is read at ordinations in many churches.

views.H: Paul's movements match 2 Corinthians and Romans: Macedonia, Corinth (where he wrote Romans), and a journey to Jerusalem with the collection about AD 57. The list of delegates includes men known from his letters (Aristarchus, Tychicus, Trophimus, Timothy, perhaps Sopater). Troas, Assos, Mitylene, Chios, Samos and Miletus lie on the natural coastal route, and the timing between Passover and Pentecost is realistic for a small coasting ship.
views.C: Many critical scholars, following Martin Dibelius, see the Miletus speech as Luke's composition, addressed to the church of his own day: the warnings about wolves and false teachers (20:29–30) and the picture of elders as overseers reflect the end of the first century. Others (F. F. Bruce, Colin Hemer) point to how Pauline its language is: "serving the Lord," humility, tears, the race, grace, self-support, and the church of God. Luke's near silence about the collection, which Paul's letters make central, is a puzzle either way.
views.L: Luke shapes Paul's journey to Jerusalem to echo Jesus' journey in the Gospel: a resolute departure (19:21; Luke 9:51), predictions of suffering (20:23; Luke 18:31–33), a farewell speech to leaders (20:18–35; Luke 22:14–38), and kneeling prayer (20:36; Luke 22:41). The Eutychus story places a raising from death on the first day of the week, at the breaking of bread, as in Luke 24.
views.J: Paul times his travel by the Jewish calendar, leaving after Unleavened Bread and hurrying for Pentecost, and carries his Gentile churches' gift to the Jewish believers of Jerusalem. The speech calls the church "the flock" and "the church of God," language that once described Israel (Psalm 74:2). Jewish readers have also noted that "the Jews" again appear as plotters (20:3, 19), and that Luke uses the phrase for particular opponents, not the whole people.
views.T: The chapter is a foundation text for church order: elders called overseers (bishops) and shepherds (pastors), appointed by the Holy Spirit. Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches read it within the later threefold ministry; Presbyterians and Baptists read it as proof that elders and bishops are one office. 20:7 is cited for Sunday worship and weekly communion, and 20:28 for the divinity of Christ ("the blood of God" in Ignatius and the fathers).

deep.h: The Miletus speech and Paul's letters
deep.b:
Of all the speeches in Acts, this one sounds most like Paul's letters. Its themes and words appear in them again and again:

  • serving the Lord as a slave, with humility (20:19; Romans 1:1; 12:11; Philippians 2:3);
  • tears and trials in Asia (20:19, 31; 2 Corinthians 1:8–10; 2:4);
  • declaring the whole message openly and from house to house, holding nothing back (20:20, 27; 1 Thessalonians 2:1–12);
  • finishing the race and the ministry received from the Lord (20:24; 1 Corinthians 9:24–27; Philippians 3:12–14; 2 Timothy 4:7);
  • the gospel of the grace of God (20:24, 32; Galatians 1:6; Romans 3:24);
  • working with his own hands so as not to burden anyone, and helping the weak (20:33–35; 1 Thessalonians 2:9; 1 Corinthians 4:12; 9:12–18);
  • the church of God (20:28; 1 Corinthians 1:2; 10:32; 11:22).

Scholars explain the likeness in two main ways. Some think Luke, a companion who heard Paul speak (this is a "we" section), gives a faithful summary. Others think Luke, who knew Paul's way of speaking well, composed the speech to present Paul's legacy to the church of his own time, as Greek historians composed speeches (Thucydides 1.22 describes the practice). Many hold a combination of both.

In 20:17 Luke calls the leaders "elders" (presbyteroi). In 20:28 Paul calls the same men "overseers" (episkopoi) and tells them "to shepherd" (poimainein) the church. The same overlap appears in Titus 1:5–7 and 1 Peter 5:1–2. By about AD 110, Ignatius of Antioch writes to Ephesus and other churches of Asia assuming one bishop in each city, with presbyters and deacons under him. How the single bishop emerged from a group of elder-overseers, and whether that development was guided by God and binding on later churches, is one of the deepest divisions between the churches (see the card below). Jerome, writing about AD 400, noted that in the apostles' time elders and bishops were the same, and that the single bishop was set over the rest to prevent division (Letter 146).

deep.title: Claude's theory: an Easter night at Troas
deep.b: The Eutychus story has the shape of Luke's Easter chapter. In Luke 24 it is the first day of the week; disciples are gathered; the risen Jesus explains the Scriptures at length; he is known "in the breaking of the bread"; and death turns out to be overcome. At Troas it is the first day of the week; the believers gather "to break bread"; Paul speaks at length; a young man dies and is given back alive; then bread is broken and the talk goes on until dawn, the hour of the first Easter. My suggestion is that Luke tells the story so that his readers, who met on the same day for the same meal, would see their own gathering as a meeting with the risen Lord, where death does not have the last word. Scholars have noted the Elijah and Elisha parallels and the link with the Lord's Supper; reading the scene as a deliberate echo of Luke 24's Easter pattern is my own proposal.

echoes: Genesis 49; Deuteronomy 31–33; Joshua 23–24; 1 Samuel 12:1–5; Numbers 16:15; 1 Kings 17:17–24; 2 Kings 4:32–37; Psalm 74:2; Ezekiel 3:17–21; Ezekiel 33:1–9; Ezekiel 34; Matthew 7:15; Luke 22:14–38; Luke 24:13–35; John 10:11–16; John 21:15–17; 1 Corinthians 16:1–4; 2 Corinthians 8–9; Romans 15:25–31; 1 Thessalonians 2:1–12; 1 Peter 5:1–4; Titus 1:5–7

settings.to: the disciples at Ephesus, then the churches of Macedonia
settings.when: after the riot, about AD 55–56
settings.why: to strengthen young churches before he left the region for good, and (as his letters show) to gather the collection for Jerusalem
settings.readers: Luke's readers knew these churches, or churches like them, as the fruit of Paul's work.

settings.what: Paul's all-night talk at Troas, and the raising of Eutychus
settings.by: Paul (with his words to the crowd in 20:10)
settings.to: the believers of Troas gathered in an upstairs room on the first day of the week
settings.when: on Paul's last night before sailing, about AD 57
settings.why: to teach a church he would not see again; and, when Eutychus fell, to calm the mourners and give the young man back alive
settings.readers: Luke's readers (Theophilus and the churches he wrote for), who met on the same day for the same meal, saw the risen Lord's power present at their own gatherings.

settings.to: the elders (overseers) of the church of Ephesus, summoned to Miletus
settings.when: on his way to Jerusalem with the collection, a few weeks before Pentecost, about AD 57; he expected never to see them again
settings.why: to defend his conduct among them (no greed, no hidden teaching), to prepare them for his coming imprisonment, and to hand over to them the care of the church: watch yourselves, shepherd God's flock, resist false teachers, work hard and help the weak
settings.readers: For Luke's readers (after Paul's death if Acts was written late, or shortly before it if early), the speech was Paul's testament to the church of their own day: a charge to its elders to shepherd the flock, and a warning about the wolves he foresaw.
views: Luke, present in this "we" section, gives a faithful summary of what Paul said (Bruce, Hemer).
Luke composed the speech to present Paul's legacy to the church of his own time (Dibelius, Haenchen, Pervo).

settings.what: A saying of the Lord Jesus: "Giving is more blessed than receiving"
settings.to: first Jesus' own hearers (the occasion is unknown); here the Ephesian elders
settings.when: the saying was handed down by word of mouth before any Gospel was written
settings.why: to ground the elders' duty to work and help the weak in the Lord's own words, so that leadership would mean giving, not taking
settings.readers: Luke's readers learned that the church remembered more of Jesus' teaching than the Gospels record, and that it was meant to be lived, not only repeated.

settings.what: Paul's farewell prayer with the elders
settings.by: Paul, kneeling with all the elders
settings.to: God (Luke does not record the words)
settings.when: at the end of the speech at Miletus, just before Paul boarded ship, about AD 57
settings.why: to commit the elders and the church to God, as he had just said he was doing (20:32), at a parting he expected to be final
settings.readers: Luke's readers saw a church that faced danger and parting on its knees. Kneeling to pray marks other key moments in Luke's story: Jesus on the Mount of Olives (Luke 22:41), Stephen (7:60), Peter at Joppa (9:40), and the farewell at Tyre (21:5).

traditions.q: The believers at Troas gathered "on the first day of the week... to break bread" (20:7). How often should the church celebrate the Lord's Supper?
views: The Eucharist is celebrated every day, and the Sunday Eucharist is the heart of the Church's life; Catholics are obliged to take part in Mass on Sundays and holy days (Catechism 2177, 2181).

The Divine Liturgy is celebrated every Sunday and on feasts. How often lay people receive communion has varied over the centuries; many Orthodox churches now encourage frequent communion with preparation by prayer, fasting and confession.

The Augsburg Confession says that among Lutherans the Mass is held on Sundays and other festivals, with the sacrament offered to those who wish to receive it (article 24). Lutheran churches today increasingly celebrate it every Sunday.

Calvin taught that the Supper should be held "at least once a week" (Institutes 4.17.43–46), but Geneva's council allowed only four times a year. Reformed and Presbyterian churches vary, from weekly to quarterly; many hold it monthly.

Churches of Christ and the Christian Churches celebrate the Lord's Supper every Sunday, taking Acts 20:7 as the apostolic example that the church should follow (Alexander Campbell, The Christian System).

John Wesley taught that it is every Christian's duty to receive the Lord's Supper "as often as he can" (The Duty of Constant Communion) and himself received it often. Methodist churches today range from weekly to monthly.
The Lord's Supper is an ordinance of remembrance; each congregation decides how often to keep it (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article VII). Many celebrate it monthly or quarterly, some weekly.

traditions.q: Paul called the Ephesian "elders" (20:17) "overseers" (20:28), the word later rendered "bishops." Are bishops a separate order above presbyters (priests), or are bishops and elders one office?
views: The ordained ministry has three degrees: bishops, priests (presbyters) and deacons. The New Testament words were not yet fixed, but the bishops are the successors of the apostles by divine institution, and this order was in place by the time of Ignatius (Lumen Gentium 20–21; Catechism 1554–1555).

The threefold ministry of bishop, presbyter and deacon is apostolic, and the bishop, in succession from the apostles, is the center of each local church's unity. The overlap of words in Acts 20 belongs to the first generation, before the offices were distinguished in name.

"It is evident unto all men diligently reading the holy Scripture and ancient Authors, that from the Apostles' time there have been these Orders of Ministers in Christ's Church; Bishops, Priests, and Deacons" (Preface to the Ordinal, 1662). Anglicans differ on whether the episcopate is necessary to the church or only for its well-being.

By divine right bishops and pastors are the same; the higher rank of bishops is by human arrangement, as Jerome noted (Treatise on the Power and Primacy of the Pope, 60–65). Some Lutheran churches keep bishops, and some keep the historic succession.

Scripture uses "bishops," "presbyters" and "pastors" for the same office (Calvin, Institutes 4.3.8). Presbyterian churches are governed by elders (teaching and ruling elders) meeting together, without bishops over them.

John Wesley became convinced that bishops and presbyters are one order, and on that basis he ordained elders for America in 1784 (letter "To Our Brethren in America"). Methodist bishops in many churches are elders set apart for a larger office, not a separate order.

A church's scriptural officers are "pastors and deacons" (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article VI); pastor, elder and overseer name one office. Some Baptist churches have several elders, others one pastor.
